1.title: the greeting that is a wish
1.hook: the greeting that is a wish; s-l-m — salaam, Muslim, Islam
1.howItsDone: Muslims greet one another with "as-salamu alaykum" (peace be upon you) and answer "wa alaykum as-salam" (and upon you peace), often adding "and the mercy of God and His blessings." The greeting is also said to close each daily prayer.

segments.voice: Maybe you've heard it in a shop, or at an airport gate, or across a family dinner table. Two people meet, and before anything else, before how are you, before the weather, one of them says: as-salamu alaykum. And the other one answers straight back: wa alaykum as-salam. It happens so fast it sounds like hello. It isn't hello. Hello is a noise we make to say I see you. This greeting is a wish. It hands the other person something. And the word at the center of it is one of the oldest and biggest words in the whole language of this path. It's hiding inside the name of the faith itself. Today's word is that one.
screen: `AS-SALAMU ALAYKUM.` → `IT SOUNDS LIKE HELLO.` → `IT'S A WISH.`

segments.voice: Salaam means peace. As-salamu alaykum means peace be upon you. Not I hope you're well. Peace, upon you, now. It's a gift given in the first second of meeting someone. Here's the thing almost nobody hears. Arabic builds its words from roots, usually three letters. This one is s, l, m. Put different vowels around it and you get salaam: peace. You get Islam: the surrender, the making of peace with God. And you get Muslim: a person who does that. So the name of the faith and the everyday greeting grow from the same root. Every time two Muslims say hello, they're saying a piece of the faith's own name to each other. Hebrew has the same root, which is why Jewish friends say shalom. The Qur'an even gives the word to God. Among God's names, in the fifty-ninth surah, is As-Salam: Peace itself. And the Qur'an sets a rule for greetings. In Pickthall's old translation of the fourth surah it reads: "When ye are greeted with a greeting, greet ye with a better than it or return it." So there's a small art to answering. If someone says peace be upon you, the minimum is to give it back. Better is to add something: and upon you peace, and the mercy of God, and His blessings. The greeting grows as it goes around. There's also a well-known hadith, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in Sahih Muslim, that ties the greeting to love itself. In it he tells his companions they won't truly love one another until they spread salaam among themselves. Not a feeling first and then a greeting. The greeting first, and the love grows from it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Think of one person you'll see today. Breathe in slowly. And on the way out, if you want to, send them the word, in your head. Salaam. Peace, upon you. You don't have to say it out loud. Just mean it once.
Salaam. Peace. The greeting that's a gift, and the root inside Islam and Muslim. First word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: peace, upon you. Today, when someone greets you, give back a little more than you got. A fuller hello, a real smile, their name. Answer with better. That's day one. See you tomorrow.

2.title: the words before every beginning
2.hook: the words before every beginning — a meal, a drive, an exam
2.howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating, drinking, setting out, studying and many small daily tasks, and the full line, bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim, is recited before reading the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: salaam. Peace, upon you. A wish, not a hello. Did you manage to mean it once, even if all that came out was hi? Day two.

Watch someone at a Muslim family's table. Before the first bite, under the breath, fast: bismillah. Watch a driver turn the key. A student turn over the first page of an exam. A mother lifting a baby out of the bath. A kid about to jump off the high dive. It may be the most-said opening in the Muslim world, and most of the time you'd miss it. It's barely a word. A breath's worth of sound before the thing begins. But it quietly changes what the thing is. Today: the words before every beginning.
screen: `BEFORE THE FIRST BITE.` → `BEFORE THE KEY TURNS.` → `A BREATH BEFORE THE THING BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Bismillah is the short form. The full line is bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim, and the old Pickthall translation of the Qur'an gives it as “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.” Bi: in, or with. Ism: name. Allah: God. Allah isn't the name of a separate god; it's the Arabic word for God, and Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews say it too. Here's the count that surprises people. The Qur'an has a hundred and fourteen chapters, called surahs. All but one open with this line. The one that doesn't is the ninth, and scholars have offered reasons why. But the line still appears a hundred and fourteen times, because the missing one turns up inside another surah, the twenty-seventh, at the top of a letter Solomon sends to a queen in the land of Sheba. So what does it do? Starting in someone's name means you're not starting alone, and not only for yourself. Think of working under someone's name, or signing a letter on someone's behalf. The work carries their name now, so it had better be worth carrying. That's why Muslims say it before ordinary things far more often than grand ones. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once told a boy eating beside him: say bismillah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you. Both Bukhari and Muslim record it. And for the times you forget, because everyone forgets, another hadith gives a way back in: say it when you remember, in the name of God at its beginning and its end. Nobody gets locked out of their own lunch.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF GOD.` · `ALL SURAHS BUT ONE OPEN WITH IT.` · `A NAME THE WORK CARRIES.` · `FORGOT? SAY IT WHEN YOU REMEMBER.` · then, large: `BISMILLAH.`

segments.voice: One breath, with the bell. Think of the very next thing you'll do after this. Making coffee. Opening an email. Starting the car. Breathe in slowly. And as the breath goes out, if you want, say the word for that next thing: bismillah. Or simply pause, one full breath, before you begin it. The pause is the part anyone can keep.
Bismillah. In the name of God. The words before a beginning, so that nothing starts alone. Second word.
Your line: start in the name of. Once today, before something ordinary, stop for one breath before you begin. A meal is the easiest place to try it. Day two.

3.title: thank-you as a reflex
3.howItsDone: Muslims say alhamdulillah when asked how they are, after meals, after sneezing, and at good news and hard news alike; after the prayer many repeat it thirty-three times, counting on their fingers or prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bismillah. In the name of God, said before a beginning. Did one ordinary thing get a breath before it started? Day three.

Ask a Muslim friend how they are. There's a good chance the first word back isn't fine. It's alhamdulillah. Got the job? Alhamdulillah. Didn't get the job? Very often, also alhamdulillah. Someone sneezes: alhamdulillah. A player scores and drops to the grass. A grandmother, asked about her knees, which are terrible: alhamdulillah. It comes out so fast it sounds like a reflex. It is one. But it's a reflex people choose to build, on purpose, and it points somewhere that surprises people. Today: the thank-you that isn't quite a thank-you.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU?` → `GOT THE JOB. DIDN'T GET THE JOB.` → `THE SAME WORD, EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Al-hamdu li-llah. Al: the. Hamd: praise. Li-llah: belongs to God. The praise belongs to God. Not thanks, God, exactly. Arabic has a separate word for thanks, shukr, and scholars draw the line between the two with care. Thanks answers something done for you. Praise answers who someone is. You can only give thanks for the good day. You can give praise on any day. That's why the word keeps showing up on the bad ones. The root of hamd, h-m-d, belongs to a family you've already heard of. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ carries it in his name: Muhammad means the one who is praised, again and again. Ahmad, Mahmoud, Hamid: the same three letters. The phrase sits near the very top of the Qur'an, right after the bismillah. We'll open that line together in a few days. And it's woven into the day. A hadith in Bukhari says: when you sneeze, say alhamdulillah, and whoever hears you answers, may God have mercy on you. After the prayer, many Muslims count it thirty-three times, on their fingers or on prayer beads. Sunni Muslims usually say it between two other short phrases; Shia Muslims say it in a sequence named for Fatima, the Prophet's daughter. Different orders, the same word. And a hadith in Muslim's collection explains why it fits any kind of day. The Prophet said the believer's situation is a wonder: when good comes, they're grateful, and that's good for them; when hardship comes, they're patient, and that's good for them too. Alhamdulillah is the two-second version. It doesn't pretend the bad day was good. It says the praise still belongs where it belonged this morning.

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of one thing that went right today. On the second, one thing that didn't. On the third, hold both at once, the good one and the hard one, and notice they belong to the same day. If you want, let the word ride out on that last breath: alhamdulillah.
Alhamdulillah. The praise belongs to God. Praise, not only thanks, so it fits every kind of day. Third word.
Your line: praise, whatever the day did. Tonight, before you sleep, name one thing from today worth praising, even if the day mostly wasn't. Day three.

4.title: not "maybe"
4.tomorrow: plainly, in one session, as a shape not a checklist
4.howItsDone: Muslims add inshallah, "if God wills," whenever they speak of something they intend to do in the future, from meeting a friend tomorrow to a plan years away, following Qur'an 18:23–24.

segments.voice: Yesterday: alhamdulillah. Praise, whatever the day did. What did you find to praise last night? A small one counts. Day four.

See you tomorrow? Inshallah. Will the report be done by Friday? Inshallah. Are we going to the beach this summer? Inshallah. If you've spent time around Muslim families, you know the joke, and Muslims tell it about themselves: inshallah is the politest way to say probably not. Kids learn early to hear the difference between yes and inshallah. It's a good joke. But it's a joke about how people use the word. The word itself is doing something else, something much older and much more serious about tomorrow.
screen: `SEE YOU TOMORROW? INSHALLAH.` → `THE FAMILY JOKE: PROBABLY NOT.` → `THE WORD MEANS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: In sha' Allah. In: if. Sha'a: wills. Allah: God. If God wills. It comes straight from the Qur'an, from the eighteenth surah, called the Cave. Pickthall's translation reads: “And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow,” and the next verse goes on, “Except if Allah will.” Then it adds: remember your Lord when you forget. Early biographies of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tell a story about these verses: that he was asked some hard questions, promised the answers for the next day without adding if God wills, and the revelation he was waiting for was delayed. Historians treat that as a report from those early biographies, not as settled fact. The verses themselves are plain. So inshallah isn't maybe. Maybe is about your mood. Inshallah is about what you don't control. You can intend something completely, plan it to the minute, and still admit that tomorrow isn't yours to hand out. And it was never meant as a reason to skip the work. There's a well-known hadith in al-Tirmidhi's collection: a man asks the Prophet whether he should leave his camel untied and trust God, or tie it up and trust God. The answer: tie it, and trust. Plan. Show up. Do your part completely. Then say inshallah and mean it: I'm doing what's mine to do, and I know I'm not in charge of the whole of it. People who live by the word say it makes a promise more honest, not less. And it makes a plan that falls through a little easier to forgive.
screen: `IF GOD WILLS.` · `SAY NOT: I SHALL DO THAT TOMORROW.` · `MAYBE IS A MOOD. THIS ISN'T.` · `TIE YOUR CAMEL, AND TRUST.` · then, large: `INSHALLAH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one thing you've planned for tomorrow, big or small. First breath: see it, the way you intend it to go. Second breath: notice the part of it that's actually up to you. Third breath: notice the part that isn't, and let it be not yours. If you want, on that last breath: inshallah.
Inshallah. If God wills. Not a maybe: a whole plan, held with an open hand. Fourth word.
Your line: if it's meant. Today, when you make a plan with someone, do your part of it completely, and hold the rest a little more loosely. Day four.

5.title: plainly, in one session, as a shape not a checklist
5.hook: plainly, in one session, as a shape not a checklist
5.carry: five things that hold a life up
5.tomorrow: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful"
5.howItsDone: Muslims keep the five together: the shahada as the core of faith, the five daily prayers, zakat given yearly, the Ramadan fast, and the hajj once in a lifetime for those able. Shia Muslims keep the same practices and describe the faith as roots (beliefs) and branches (practices).

segments.voice: Yesterday: inshallah. If it's meant. A whole plan, held with an open hand. Did the thing you planned turn out the way you pictured? Day five.

Most people learn the five pillars of Islam the way you learn a list for a test. Witness. Prayer. Giving. Fasting. Pilgrimage. Five words, five boxes, done. And if that's all you have, it sounds like a checklist: tick the boxes, pass. But that isn't how the tradition itself pictures them. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described them as a building. So today, plainly, in one sitting, you get all five, not as a list but as a shape. And the shape turns out to be made of time.
screen: `FIVE WORDS, FIVE BOXES?` → `NOT A CHECKLIST.` → `A BUILDING.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in both Bukhari and Muslim: Islam is built on five. Built, like a house. Pillars are what keep the roof up. One: the shahada, the witness. There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. One sentence. Said to become Muslim, said inside every prayer, whispered to a newborn, hoped for as a last word. Its clock is always. Two: salat, prayer, five times a day, at times that move with the sun: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, night. Many Shia Muslims join them into three sittings; the prayers are still five. Its clock is the day. Three: zakat, giving a share of what you have to people in need, counted once a year; in Sunni practice usually two and a half percent of savings. Four: sawm, fasting from dawn to sunset through the month of Ramadan. Their clock is the year. Five: hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime. Its clock is a life. Now look at the shape. Always. Every day. Every year. Once in a life. Circles inside circles, from a single breath out to a whole lifetime. And the house is built to fit the person living in it. The Qur'an lets the sick and the traveler make up missed fast days later, and asks for the hajj only from those able to make the journey. Muslims also draw the house in more than one way. Sunni teaching usually names these five as the pillars. Shia teaching usually speaks of roots, the core beliefs, and branches, the practices. Prayer, fasting, giving and pilgrimage sit among the branches, and the witness lives in the roots. Same house, drawn two ways.
screen: `ISLAM IS BUILT ON FIVE.` · `ALWAYS, DAILY, YEARLY, ONCE.` · `BUILT TO FIT THE PERSON.` · `ROOTS AND BRANCHES: DRAWN TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `FIVE THINGS THAT HOLD A LIFE UP.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. The pillars are circles of time, so let's borrow the shape. First breath: something that holds up your day. Second breath: something that holds up your year. Third breath: something you'd want to do once in your life. You don't have to do anything about them yet. Just see what's holding you up.
The five pillars. Witness, prayer, giving, fasting, pilgrimage. Not five boxes but a house built on five. Fifth word.
Your line: five things that hold a life up. Today, notice one thing you do every day that you'd miss if it fell. Day five.

6.title: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful"
6.hook: the opening — seven verses said seventeen times a day, and the first is a name
6.carry: in the name of the merciful
6.tomorrow: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"
6.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and at many other moments: over the sick, at a wedding, for someone who has died. When it ends in prayer, most Sunni Muslims say amin; Shia Muslims of the Ja'fari school do not say amin in the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five pillars. Five things that hold a life up, on clocks from a breath to a lifetime. Which one did you notice holding yours? Day six.
screen: `THE FIVE PILLARS — ALWAYS, DAILY, YEARLY, ONCE.`

segments.voice: Think of the thing you've said most often in your life. Your own name. Hello. Probably I'm fine. Now picture a prayer seven verses long, said seventeen times every day in the required prayers, by a child of seven and a woman of ninety, in a desert, a city apartment, an airport corner. Over a lifetime, that's hundreds of thousands of times. Whatever that prayer says, it's going to wear a groove in a person. It's called al-Fatiha. For the next seven days, we'll walk through it one verse a day. And the first verse is one you already know.
screen: `SEVEN VERSES.` → `SEVENTEEN TIMES A DAY.` → `ONE VERSE A DAY, FOR SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Al-Fatiha means the opening. It's the first surah of the Qur'an, and its root, f-t-h, is the root of opening things: a door, a way, a city. The Arabic word for a key, miftah, grows from it too. The Qur'an speaks of seven oft-repeated verses, and many scholars read that as al-Fatiha. A hadith in Bukhari says there is no prayer without it. That's where the seventeen comes from: the five daily prayers add up to seventeen units, and every unit begins with these seven verses. Now, verse one. In the numbering Pickthall follows, and most printed copies of the Qur'an today, the first verse is the line you met on day two. In his words: “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.” Bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim. On day two it was the words before a meal or a drive. Here it's the first step into the prayer itself. Listen to the shape of it. The prayer doesn't open with a request, or with the one praying at all. It opens by stepping inside a name, the way you'd walk through a door someone is holding. Everything after this is said in that name. And which name? Not the powerful one, not the judge. The two names chosen for the doorway are both mercy. We'll open those two words properly on day eight. For today, just notice where the most repeated prayer in a Muslim's life begins: in a name, and the name is merciful. Verse one of seven.
screen: `THE OPENING — F-T-H, A KEY.` · `NO PRAYER WITHOUT IT.` · `VERSE ONE: THE DAY-TWO LINE.` · `THROUGH THE DOOR OF A NAME.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF THE MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Picture a doorway in front of you, and someone kind holding the door. First breath: stand at the threshold. Second breath: step through. Third breath: notice that whatever you do next, you're doing it from inside. If you want, let the line go out with the last breath: bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim.
Al-Fatiha. The opening: seven verses at the start of the Qur'an, and at the start of every unit of every prayer. Sixth word.
Your line: in the name of the merciful. Today, begin one conversation that could go either way with the gentlest first sentence you have. Day six.

fork.setup: someone new to the prayer knows very little Arabic yet. which part does a hadith in Bukhari say no prayer can be without?
options: the longest surah you know.
al-Fatiha.
any verse at all.
fork.reveal: there is no prayer without al-Fatiha. that's why it's usually among the first things a learner memorizes.

original.note: Arabic: "the opening." from f-t-h, to open, the same root as miftah, a key.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first chapter, like a preface.
what it means: the opening — seven verses said in every unit of every prayer, beginning in a merciful name.

what a scholar hears: the Qur'an's "seven oft-repeated" (15:87) is widely read as al-Fatiha; whether the bismillah is its first verse depends on the verse count, and the schools differ on reciting it aloud.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 756; Sahih Muslim 394 (no prayer without al-Fatiha)

7.title: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"
7.hook: the lord who raises and tends every world, not just yours
7.howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and many say alhamdulillah, its opening word, many times a day. Rabb is also the word Muslims use in many personal prayers, often as Rabbi, my Lord, or Rabbana, our Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Fatiha, the opening, and its first verse, a doorway made of a name. Your line was in the name of the merciful. Did a gentle first sentence help? Day seven.

A week ago this started with one word. Salaam. Since then: bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah, the five pillars, and the opening of a prayer. Here's something you might not have noticed. Two of those words were already waiting inside that prayer. Bismillah is its first verse. And alhamdulillah is the very first word of the second. So today, as the week closes, the week comes back to meet us. Verse two takes the thank-you you learned on day three and points it somewhere enormous. Not at your day. At every world there is.
screen: `A WEEK OF WORDS.` → `BISMILLAH: VERSE ONE.` → `ALHAMDULILLAH: VERSE TWO.`

segments.voice: Verse two, in Pickthall's words: “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” In Arabic, al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin. The first half is your day-three word, alhamdulillah. The small al- at the front makes it all praise, every kind, belonging to God. Now the new word. Rabb. English usually says Lord, and that's right, but it's thin. Rabb is the one who owns and the one who looks after. Classical commentators explain it with the picture of raising something: bringing a child, or a seedling, along step by step until it's grown. So a rabb isn't a distant owner with paperwork. It's the one who feeds, shelters and brings you up. And then: al-'alamin. The worlds. Not the world, the worlds, plural. Commentators have listed people, angels, animals, every kind of created thing; some say each kind is a world of its own. The ant colony under the sidewalk. The deep sea. The inside of a stranger's life on the train. All of it, the verse says, is being raised and tended by one Rabb. There's a lovely detail from a hadith qudsi, a saying of God reported by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and recorded by Muslim. It describes al-Fatiha as a conversation. When someone praying says this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me. So the thank-you from day three isn't said into empty air. In the prayer, it's heard, and answered. Two verses down, five to go.
screen: `ALHAMDULILLAH — ALL PRAISE.` · `RABB — THE ONE WHO RAISES.` · `AL-'ALAMIN — THE WORLDS, PLURAL.` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME.` · then, large: `EVERY WORLD IS TENDED.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. First breath: your own world. One thing in it that's being looked after, even today. Second breath: a world that isn't yours. A bird, a stranger, a field somewhere you'll never see. Third breath: hold both at once. If you want, the Arabic rides out on the last one: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin.
Rabb. Lord: the one who owns, raises and looks after, here the Lord of all the worlds. Seventh word, and a full week on your strand.
Your line: every world is tended. Today, notice one small world that isn't yours, a plant on a windowsill, a neighbor's routine, and whatever keeps it going. A week, done. Day seven.

fork.setup: someone praying says: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. in the hadith qudsi recorded by Muslim, what happens next?
options: nothing: prayer is a one-way message.
God answers: My servant has praised Me.
the angels repeat it back.
fork.reveal: the hadith describes al-Fatiha as a conversation. at this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me.

original.note: Arabic: lord, master, the one who raises and looks after. in al-Fatiha: rabbi l-'alamin, Lord of the Worlds.

trapdoor: what you thought: "Lord" — a title, like a king's.
what it means: the one who owns and looks after, raising every world along.
what a scholar hears: commentators gloss rabb with tarbiya, bringing a thing gradually to completion; al-'alamin, plural of 'alam, is read as every class of creation.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 395 (the hadith qudsi of al-Fatiha as a conversation)
